query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The stability of near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the synthesis annealing profile, which controls whether the nanoparticles remain kinetically trapped in a high-entropy, homogeneous state or undergo thermally activated atomic diffusion that leads to elemental segregation and nano‐precipitate formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles produced via physical or chemical synthesis that initially exhibit a kinetically trapped, homogeneous (metastable) solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal annealing protocol with varying dwell times and cooling rates (e.g., rapid quenching versus slow cooling) at temperatures within or near the service regimes.
generation.conditions: Annealing treatments performed at predetermined temperatures (e.g., between 773 K and 1173 K for catalytic applications and 473 K to 1923 K for thermoelectric applications) with systematically varied dwell times and cooling rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic-scale configurational disorder retained versus the onset of localized atomic diffusion and aggregation that leads to phase segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.mechanism: Short, rapid annealing maintains high configurational entropy by limiting the time available for atomic diffusion, thereby preserving the metastable, homogeneous structure. In contrast, prolonged annealing or slow cooling provides sufficient thermal energy and time for atoms to overcome kinetic barriers, promoting elemental segregation and the formation of secondary phases that compromise chemical and structural stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles subjected to rapid thermal annealing (short dwell time and fast cooling) will show a more uniform elemental distribution and sustained structural stability under high-temperature service testing, while those exposed to longer dwell times or slower cooling will exhibit signs of segregation (e.g., nano-precipitate formation) and deteriorated catalytic/thermoelectric performance relative to their baseline state.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles fabricated using typical synthesis routes without controlled thermal treatment, which tend to develop heterogeneous microstructures and show premature phase separation under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic relationship is expected to hold for near-equiatomic, kinetically trapped nanoparticles without additional stabilization (such as high noble-metal content) and within service temperature ranges where thermally activated diffusion becomes significant. Extremely high temperatures or alternative alloy systems might exhibit different behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative thresholds (e.g., critical dwell times and cooling rates) at which the balance shifts from kinetic trapping to diffusion-driven segregation remain uncertain and likely depend on specific elemental properties such as atomic radii and bonding preferences.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a batch of near-equiatomic nanoparticles under identical initial conditions and divide them into groups. Subject each group to different thermal annealing protocols varying in dwell time (e.g., 5 seconds, 1 minute, 10 minutes) and cooling rate (rapid quench vs. gradual cooling) at service-relevant temperatures. After annealing, simulate prolonged exposure to high-temperature conditions and assess structural integrity.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase composition and detect secondary phases.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for nanoscale imaging and mapping of elemental distribution.
Performance metrics under catalytic/thermoelectric stress tests to evaluate functional stability.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If rapid annealing protocols do not result in statistically significant improvements in maintaining a homogeneous, metastable solid-solution structure—and if both rapid and prolonged annealing treatments show similar levels of elemental segregation and performance degradation—then the hypothesis that the synthesis annealing profile governs structural and chemical stability through kinetic trapping will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials performance is central to the satisfactory operation of current and future nuclear energy systems due to the severe irradiation environment in reactors. Searching for structural materials with excellent irradiation tolerance is crucial for developing the next generation nuclear reactors. Here, we report the irradiation responses of a novel multi-component alloy system, high entropy alloy (HEA) Al x CoCrFeNi ( x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5), focusing on their precipitation behavior. It is found that the single phase system, Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi, exhibits a great phase stability against ion irradiation. No precipitate is observed even at the highest fluence. In contrast, numerous coherent precipitates are present in both multi-phase HEAs. Based on the irradiation-induced/enhanced precipitation theory, the excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion, which reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrains the formation of precipitate, respectively. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

chosen.why: This move most directly fills the gap in our understanding of the synthesis–structure–property relationships. By precisely controlling the thermal processing (annealing profiles) and applying in-situ characterization tools, the study can directly test the mechanistic hypothesis that proper thermal locking of the high-entropy state (or failure thereof) governs whether phase segregation and chemical instability occur under relevant service conditions. This approach employs standard, well‐established techniques in materials science to resolve the open question posed.

prior_attempts: Multiple fabrication approaches (both physical and chemical) have been applied to synthesize near-equiatomic nanoparticles
These attempts have yielded nanoparticles with diverse structures, but without a clear understanding of how synthesis influences stability under service conditions
frame.understanding: A plausible mechanism is that the atomic-scale configurational entropy in near-equiatomic nanoparticles promotes a kinetically trapped, metastable solid solution that resists phase separation and surface segregation at elevated temperatures. Variations in elemental bonding preferences and differences in atomic radii may however drive local ordering or elemental segregation when thermal energy overcomes the entropy stabilization. The hypothesis is testable by designing a controlled annealing experiment where the degree of elemental mixing and structural integrity is monitored as a function of time and temperature, thereby separating the effects of inherent entropy stabilization from thermally induced diffusion processes.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on multi‐element, near‐equiatomic systems began with standard fabrication routes (arc melting, sputtering, or high‐energy milling) that produced either single‐phase or multiphase structures. For example, PMC4999872 demonstrated that a low-alloyed (single-phase) HEA resists precipitate formation under extreme conditions, whereas multiphase variants tend to develop coherent nano-precipitates due to local compositional fluctuations. Later work (PMC10213035) employed controlled, stepwise thermo-mechanical processing (including short, high‐temperature annealing steps) to deliberately tailor coherent precipitation while quantifying the related changes in microstructure. These efforts highlighted that the stability of the metastable solid solution is strongly contingent on the synthesis thermal history, yet the complex interplay between inherent entropy stabilization and thermally driven diffusion (leading to elemental segregation or precipitate coarsening) remains poorly understood.
decision.unsolved: It is still not clear how specific annealing profiles control the balance between the entropy‐driven kinetic trapping of a homogeneous, metastable solid solution and the onset of thermally induced phase segregation at service temperatures. This gap in understanding prevents a predictive synthesis–structure–property relationship, particularly for nanoparticles intended for high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric applications with low noble-metal content.
decision.why: Based on the trend in previous work where controlled annealing was used to manipulate phase stability and precipitation, the most plausible next step is to design a series of rapid thermal annealing experiments that vary dwell time, peak temperature, and cooling rates. This intervention will directly isolate the kinetic window wherein the configurational entropy of near‐equiatomic nanoparticles kinetically traps the metastable solid solution versus when thermal diffusion begins to dominate, triggering phase separation. This approach occupies the niche focused on establishing synthesis–structure–property relationships and addresses the core open question regarding the mechanism governing structural and chemical stability under the relevant high-temperature conditions.
